title: UK Regulators' Captive Insurance Proposals Close for Comment on October 14, With a Regime Planned for Summer 2027
summary: The PRA and FCA want a tailored regime for single-parent captives with 4-to-6-week authorisation and lighter rules; no captive insurers are currently established in the UK.
description:
The deadline for responses to the United Kingdom's proposed captive insurance regime falls on October 14, 2026, which makes this a good moment to update a story first published in August. A captive is a wholly owned insurance subsidiary that a business uses to manage its own risks, and the FCA notes that no captive insurers are currently established in the UK. The Prudential Regulation Authority and the Financial Conduct Authority published a joint proposal on July 14 to change that. The PRA's paper is numbered CP11/26 and the FCA's is CP26/29.

The core idea is proportionality. The FCA's rationale, as set out on its consultation page, is that captives generally insure only risks within their own group, so they pose lower risks to market integrity and consumer protection than conventional insurers. The rules should therefore be lighter. According to the Bank of England's announcement, the regime would offer a streamlined joint PRA and FCA authorisation process with a target of four to six weeks. Captives would be exempt from the full Solvency UK regime and from the Consumer Duty, which is the FCA's standard for retail customer outcomes. They would face lower capital and reporting requirements and a flexible framework for what counts as capital resources. The PRA would assign dedicated supervisory resource, and the FCA would apply tailored conduct requirements with proportionate supervision and reporting.

The proposals also set limits. The regime is aimed at single-parent captives, meaning those that insure or reinsure the risks of their own parent group. There is a safeguard on employee benefits: captives may reinsure, but not directly insure, policies related to employee benefits, which appears intended to keep individual employees from depending on a lightly regulated captive. The regulators also said that protected cell companies, which allow several risk programmes to be housed in one entity, might be the subject of a later consultation once the necessary legislation is in place.

The regulators have been explicit about the economic goal. David Bailey of the PRA said the authority is keen to speak to any businesses that could benefit from establishing a UK-based captive, and Sarah Pritchard of the FCA said the approach is pragmatic and proportionate with appropriate safeguards. The announcement's own headline ties the plan to UK growth and competitiveness. Captives are commonly domiciled in other jurisdictions, and the UK has had little presence in the market despite London's role in commercial insurance and reinsurance.

Timing matters. The consultation opened on July 14 and closes on October 14. After that the regulators will consider responses and publish a policy statement with final rules, and the Bank of England says the regime is due to launch in summer 2027. The FCA noted that its consultation page was updated on October 8 only to fix a link, so no change to the dates or substance was announced in the weeks before the deadline.

Why would a company use a captive at all? There are several reasons. A captive can allow a business to retain predictable risks, such as property damage or product liability claims, and pay itself through the subsidiary instead of paying premiums to an external insurer that includes its own profit and costs. It can give access to the reinsurance market directly, which can be cheaper than buying primary insurance for large risks. It can also centralise risk management and provide cover for risks that are hard to insure in the commercial market. The trade-off is that the parent takes on volatility and must hold capital in the captive, which is why regulators set minimum requirements.

The UK would be entering a competitive field. Established domiciles such as Bermuda, Guernsey and others have specialised regimes and experienced service providers, as the Singapore story elsewhere on this site illustrates, where the regulator is consulting on cell structures to compete in Asia. A UK regime will have to prove that fast authorisation and proportionate supervision are real in practice, and that tax, legal and operational conditions suit corporate groups. The detail on capital calibration will determine how attractive the regime is, and that detail sits in the full consultation papers.

Who should respond? The FCA lists insurers and reinsurers considering captive structures, intermediaries, captive managers, legal and actuarial advisers and trade bodies. The FCA accepts responses through an online form, and the PRA has a separate route through its Insurance Policy Division. Because the deadline is October 14, firms that have not yet engaged should act now or consider contacting the regulators directly if they need more time.

For most readers, the practical meaning is simple. If you run risk for a large UK group, a UK captive could become an option from 2027, with lower regulatory friction than a conventional insurer. If you work in insurance services, the regime could create demand for captive management, actuarial and legal work. For consumers, the effect is indirect, and the safeguard on employee benefits is intended to keep individuals from relying on a lightly regulated captive. As always, this is a proposal rather than a final rule, and the policy statements due after the consultation will set the final terms.
key_points: On July 14, 2026 the PRA (CP11/26) and FCA (CP26/29) opened a joint consultation on a tailored regime for UK captive insurers.
The consultation closes on October 14, 2026, and the regime is due to launch in summer 2027 after feedback is considered.
Proposals include a 4-to-6-week authorisation target, exemption from Solvency UK and Consumer Duty, lower capital and reporting requirements and dedicated PRA supervisors.
The regime is limited to single-parent captives, which may reinsure but not directly insure employee-benefits-related policies; protected cell companies may be consulted on later.
No captive insurers are currently established in the UK, according to the FCA.
why_it_matters: A captive lets a company finance its own risks through a regulated insurance subsidiary instead of buying all of its cover from outside insurers. A UK regime would give corporate risk managers a new domicile option and could bring insurance jobs and capital to London, but the proposal is still a consultation and the final rules could differ.
